title: Patrick McQuestion
text:
About
I am a PhD candidate in Peace Studies and Political Science at the University of Notre Dame’s Kroc Institute for International Peace Studies, where I am a Presidential Fellow in the Humanities and Social Sciences and a Doctoral Student Affiliate of the Kellogg Institute for International Studies. My dissertation, “Mining for Peace: Conflict Settlements and Extractivism in Colombia and Peru,” examines how the type of conflict settlement — negotiated partial agreements in Colombia versus military victory in Peru — shapes subnational extractive governance. Drawing on comparative historical analysis, original interviews, and archival research, my work traces how peace processes open durable channels of accountability between communities, companies, and the state, and how their absence enables more asymmetrical, sometimes criminalized, resource governance.
My research also extends into democratization studies, where I have co-developed a new method for measuring subnational democracy using Varieties of Democracy data. I also write on formalization policy, illegal mining economies, and the role of civil society — including the Catholic Church in the Peruvian Amazon — in shaping environmental politics.
Before Notre Dame, I was a Research Associate with the Kroc Institute’s Peace Accords Matrix, monitoring implementation of the 2016 Colombian peace agreement, and a Technical Analyst with Argentina’s Ministry of Modernization. I hold an M.A. in Development Management and Policy from Georgetown University and Universidad Nacional de San Martín (Argentina), and a B.A. in English from Reed College. I also coordinate the Kellogg Institute’s Global Stage podcast.

title: Research
text: My research sits at the intersection of comparative political economy and peace studies, focusing on conflict legacies, policy design, and extractive enterprises in Latin America. I am motivated to understand conflict transformation processes, the protection of human and environmental rights, and the roots of ethical political economy.

title: Research
text:
Dissertation: Mining for Peace
Conflict Settlements and Extractivism in Colombia and Peru
My dissertation examines the political and institutional dynamics of peacebuilding interventions in resource-rich environments, using Colombia as a primary case to unpack how the type of conflict settlement shapes subnational governance of extractive industries over time — and Peru as a contrasting case where no comprehensive peace process took place. Across both cases, I am developing a typology of extractive governance in conflict-affected countries, contributing to research on the political economy of developing extractive economies.
In the Colombia chapters, I use comparative historical analysis, interviews with negotiators, and archival research to interrogate the revenue-based motivations of government negotiators and insurgent or paramilitary groups in designing partial peace agreements in strategic resource-rich regions, and to ask how the localized presence of multi-cultural ethnic and campesino groups in resource-rich zones may shape accountability dynamics resembling third-party monitoring. I also examine whether this dynamic extends beyond partial agreements into the design of more comprehensive frameworks, including the 2016 agreement with the FARC-EP — tracing the decision-making behind incorporating multi-cultural populations as protagonists in truth and reconciliation processes, as arbiters of investment projects, and as guardians of the natural environments where resources are most contested.
The Peru chapter interrogates this “peace learning” hypothesis in a setting where the absence of partial or comprehensive peace processes between the government and insurgent groups may produce markedly different governance dynamics. Resource-rich areas there are highly contested by private speculators and local communities; I ask whether the absence of formal elite pacts — from which repertoires of accountability could otherwise be forged — helps explain more costly collective action, and in some cases, governance capture by criminal enterprises.

title: Research
text:
Broader Research Agenda
Measuring subnational democracy. In a co-authored project, I apply comparative area expertise in Colombia to introduce a new methodology for measuring subnational levels of democracy, combining empirical data with Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) expert survey responses. I demonstrate this method in my dissertation by comparing democracy levels across mining sites in Colombia and Peru.
Civil society and environmental politics in the Peruvian Amazon. Field research in Madre de Dios motivated a line of work on the role of the Catholic Church in organizing civic action against illegal alluvial mining and shaping environmental policy — examining how Church leaders and lay people coordinate with Indigenous groups and other religious actors to influence environmental governance.
Networks. I am affiliated with the Forests and Livelihoods: Assessment, Research, and Engagement (FLARE) network, an interdisciplinary community of scholars working on environmental sustainability, and my research has been supported by the Kellogg Institute for International Studies and the Laudato Si Institute, among others.

title: Teaching
text:
I view the university classroom as a laboratory for both academic rigor and social engagement — a space to build skills like public speaking and critical thinking alongside moments of genuine intellectual connection. My teaching is guided by the conviction that political science and peace studies can come alive in and outside the classroom, broadening students’ sense of purpose while equipping them with practical skills like data literacy and public communication. In introductory courses, I aim to bridge academic theory and real-world situations through active-learning exercises that turn abstract concepts into tangible communication and analytical skills; in advanced seminars, I prioritize methodology and the knowledge-building process, pushing students to grapple with real data and its imperfections and to develop a critical eye for research design.
This dual focus — outward-facing skills for the real world, and inward-facing mastery of technical knowledge production — is designed to appeal to diverse learning styles, from the aspiring public intellectual to the future quantitative researcher. Whether leading a large lecture or a small seminar, my goal is the same: to turn students from passive consumers of information into active contributors to their fields and to society.
